findings.issue: The draft describes enforcement mechanisms that do not exist yet. No generated Codex profiles, `.rules`, or pinned `.codex/agents` are present; MCP is empty; and MODEL_MATRIX itself says the shipping/regeneration work is pending. Today a Codex seat is constrained only by its launch-time sandbox/approval settings, system/AGENTS instructions, host permissions, and provider-side controls. The cluster bans are therefore protocol intentions, not current per-profile enforcement.
findings.suggestion: Separate governance effective-now from tooling planned-later. State explicitly that peer standing is currently prose-enforced, name the Phase 3/4 implementation wave, and define the launcher/profile/policy acceptance checks before claiming mechanical enforcement.

findings.issue: Retained role mappings still place O/director and I on Claude/Fable with Sol merely consulting, and reserve design authoring for “fable-class” sessions. Because O owns dispatch, this leaves no coherent role path for the newly asserted Sol dispatch authority. These may be routing preferences, but they currently read as eligibility restrictions.
findings.suggestion: Model eligibility separately from preference: make thinking-tier roles runtime-neutral, explicitly mark both runtimes eligible for O/I/design/ratification, and encode Fable as `preferred_runtime` where desired rather than as the only mapped actor.

findings.issue: “Operate the same tool surface” is a false present-tense capability claim. The same section records empty Codex MCP configuration and a gcloud sandbox gap, while §3a says Codex currently has no conforming async-results channel. “Seats inherit the user's whole CLI surface” is also too broad: sandbox grants, PATH, credentials, and runtime configuration determine the reachable subset.
findings.suggestion: Say “same governance standing, runtime-specific capability surface.” List only verified current capabilities, and mark profiles, MCP grants, gcloud remediation, and async completion as planned or unavailable.

findings.issue: The four-item invariant list is not sufficient or exhaustive. A write-enabled seat can destroy another seat's uncommitted work with `reset --hard`/`clean`, mutate shared refs/config/hooks through the common Git directory, corrupt heartbeat or lease state, consume another seat's mailbox cursor, or self-apply fleet guidance. None requires a merge, DDL, customer contact, or self-verdict, yet retained specs already treat each as guarded coordination state.
findings.suggestion: Either label the four bullets illustrative and reference the complete invariant owners, or add explicit categories for workspace/common-Git coordination, control-plane state, mailbox cursors, host/global configuration, and guidance-policy mutation—including their owners and ceremonies.

findings.issue: “Existing ceremonies” is unsupported for several irreversible mechanisms while the corpus admits the threat model is only planned. With verified GitHub admin and deployment/database credentials, a seat can force-push or delete refs, change branch protection/repository settings, publish packages, alter DNS/projects/billing, or disclose secrets. The live consuming contract worsens this by saying remote `gh`/API operations are “always safe,” contradicting WORKSPACE_LIFECYCLE.md:42-44.
findings.suggestion: Name the normative ceremony and owner for each external-action class, correct “remote operations are always safe,” and add secret disclosure/untrusted-code handling. Until those exist, state honestly that this blast-radius boundary is incomplete.

findings.issue: “Sol satisfies [independence] structurally” is incorrect. Runtime/model identity does not prove a fresh context; Codex seats are explicitly continuation-capable. The unqualified permission to “author and ratify” also conflicts with no-self-verdicting unless it means different session contexts for different artifacts.
findings.suggestion: Define independence using recorded session handles: author session/context must differ from reviewer and ratifier context, with fresh-thread evidence where required. Say Sol is eligible to author or ratify, but never both for the same artifact in the same context.

findings.issue: The claim that these controls are “never a statement about judgment” is a rationalization. Merge and shared-environment controls are coordination/blast-radius rules, but no-self-verdicting and actor-report rejection exist specifically because judgment and self-report can be biased or wrong. Equal application to the director and both runtimes is consistent; denying their epistemic purpose is not.
findings.suggestion: Replace the claim with: these controls are runtime-neutral and do not express a lower trust grade for either runtime; some nevertheless address fallible judgment and self-report across every actor.

findings.issue: The negative-probe warning is strong, but its procedure creates a privilege-escalation loophole. “Sandbox sized to the work” names no sizing authority, and “needs an unsandboxed control” can be read as permission for the probing seat to remove its own boundary. After two consecutive misdiagnoses, prose alone is insufficient.
findings.suggestion: Require the dispatch to carry the sandbox class and grants, have the launcher enforce them, and forbid seats from self-broadening. Record denied probes as sandbox-scoped inconclusive results; route any minimally scoped, non-mutating unsandboxed control to a named owner with provenance.

strongest_aspect: SEAT_PROTOCOL.md:369-377 explicitly retires the old read-heavy/Phase-5 write gate. The remaining “read-only” at MODEL_MATRIX.md:145 is scoped to the one-shot review lane, while the “pilot” language at lines 209-214 and 250-253 is historical review scope or an actual async-capability gap—not a general Codex standing restriction.
biggest_risk: The draft could cause operators to believe peer write authority is bounded by generated policy and complete ceremonies when those mechanisms are absent or incomplete. Conflict disclosure: this runtime benefits from the ruling, so I did not assess whether parity itself is wise and would not treat my opinion as independent evidence for that premise. The findings above concern observable text, file state, and enforcement gaps; I do not consider the conflict to make those judgments unreliable.
